blocks.x: Well, I'm Jane Julian, and this is March 13, 1971, and I'm at Paul Barnes' home at 1770 North Doris-Newis Street. Is that how you pronounce it?
That's correct. Doris-Newis? Yes, that's correct.

Yeah, and I'm interviewing him for the archive of New Orleans Jazz at Tulane University. Paul, I wanted to ask you some things. First of all, about your family. You have such an interest in family, and I don't think you've ever really been interviewed about them very much.
Well, to tell a fact, I haven't.
Uh-huh. I didn't think so, you know, because I know you and your brother are both musicians, and I was wondering, did you have other brothers and sisters who were musicians?

Yes, I had one, but he didn't take up an instrument, but he used to play a fife just like I did. Oh really? Yeah. Just the same as my oldest brother, Mealy. He's the ringleader of it. He played the fife. And during those times the fife was very popular around New Orleans. If you don't know what a fife is, it's just a little instrument with six holes in it. Something you would play like a piccolo. It didn't have keys on the side, just three little holes, but you would be surprised the music that we could get out of that. It was very popular in New Orleans. I think besides my brother Sidney, Bessier, all of them played, played those little fife. And I actually started playing them when I was six years old.
Oh that's young. Well how old was your other brother? Was he older than you?
They were both older than me.
Oh, I never knew you had another brother.

I did. He was accidentally killed. Accidentally shot. Really? Yeah. All through it. He was trying to stop a fight and he accidentally got shot. Really? Oh that's sad. It was sad. But he was three years old than I.
Oh he was?
Now Mealy, he's just about ten years, pretty near ten years older than me.
What was your other brother's name? My other brother was named Andrew. Andrew. Andrew.

Andrew Barnes. We used to call him, everybody called him Boose. Boose? Yeah, Boose. It was B-O-S-E Boose. Nicknames were very popular in New Orleans at that time. And Mealy, his name is Emil. They called him Mealy. And my name being Paul, they called me Polo. Well Polo is just the same as Paul. Yeah, I understand. Everybody by the name of Paul during those times, they called him Polo.
Really? Everybody.
Once Polo's there. And I remember on in Ron Wallens, it was like you, someone named Richard and you called him Dick or James, Jim, you know so forth. You understand?

Yeah, I understand. Excuse me, Paul. Let's stop a minute and check in. Okay. Well, I think the volume and everything sounds fine, so I think we can let it stay right there. You know, and just keep on talking, which is fine with me. Well, that's fascinating. You know, I never, I read the interview you had at Tulane, the interview they did with you and Mealy. Yeah. And then one that Barry Martin did and you never mentioned another brother. You know, you mentioned, I think you mentioned your father, I think.
Well, there's still another brother between Mealy and Andrew. Oh yeah? And that's Adam. See, they all passed away except me and I'm the one last. But actually, it was Emiel, after Emiel came Emily.
Oh, you had a sister.
After Emily came Adam. After Adam came Andrew. That's what I told her, that's called Boose. Now after Andrew came Alice. Then after Alice came.
Came you. Oh, you're the youngest.
Youngest of the world. Come, come right here? Not being here, huh?
Yeah. Well I thought maybe Mealy was the only family you had. I'm real surprised to hear that. You had a big family.

Yeah, I had a big family. And my mother had another child after me and she lost it. It didn't live long. It was Francis the name was. Yeah, she was the youngest of all. But she wasn't very old? She didn't live long? No, she was just a little girl. About four or five years old. Oh, you remember her then? Oh yeah. Yeah, that's sad.

Well I know that everybody in your mother's family were musicians, you know they're related to all of the Mareros and the Frazier's and everybody. But who in your father's family was interested in music? Was your father interested?

My father was, he could play music also, it was on both sides. He used to play a guitar, but not in a band, you know. He played around the house and played guitar and singing. There was a musical there on both sides. And my mother's sister, she was very musical too, she played the guitar. Now that's, Lawrence Moreira is what I'm speaking about. Now they had Simon Moreira, he played bass like his father. Billy Moreira. People used to say Billy Moran. But it was Billy Moran. Then Simon. And the next boy was John. I'm speaking with my mother's sister's children, I don't get confused. And after John came Lawrence, then came Eddie, and then William. William didn't play instruments, but all the rest of them, Simon, John, played Simon bass. John, guitar, Lawrence played guitar and banjo, and Eddie played bass. Eddie is the last one, he's still living, but he quit playing music. So, you know, young ones take that for the old ones. That's why all my sisters' side, they were all string sections. My mother's side, they were instrumentalists. Yeah, it appears that way. It sure does. But you said your father played guitar. Yeah, he played guitar. But he didn't play, he was a musician, he played band. He played like for the family? Family and all that's like. So it was actually on musical on both sides.
Well did your father encourage you all to play music? Or did he?

Well no he did not, because my father left home when I was about six years old. Oh you were that young. He never came back home anymore. So the fact is I just don't know where Millie picked it up at. But if Millie had picked up a trombone, then why not that be a trombone player? He picked up a trumpet, I did a trumpet player. Now the other brother was Reza-Mo, that was her oldest brother. And his children played music. Now he had, we call him Sam Frazier. Shuganu, nickname. Shuganu. He was a drum player. He was old, he'd be with my older brother. He was a drum player. And then after Shuganu, the next brother was Josiah. They called him Saeed. Well I know him. Well Saeed, that's the other son. That's from the oldest brother. Then after Saeed came, he was one of the first, Elek. Elek Frazier. And he was a good, he played piano. Then after Elek came Simon Frazier. Now that's from the older brother. Now the other brother, my mother's third brother, was Michelle Frazier. His children were very much interested in music too, but the only one that went out was Mitchell. Most all the musicians around the world, they know Mitchell Frazier. That's from my mother's youngest brother. And he was a real good piano player. So that's where on the Frazier side, they have more of them than on the Barnes. Now my mother, quite exactly, she married a Barnes and we come out of Barnes. And her sister, Jeannette, married a Marrera. And so that came, he was a bass player. So Lawrence Marrera and Eddie Marrera, they came out playing music. See, from my mother's sister. Now the other ones I was telling you about was my mother's brother, but now I'm telling you about the sister. She married a Marrera, and the Marrera's came out. So you see how that family of music, you know, it's just in the whole

family. Oh yeah, I can see that easily. And I knew, you know, I knew from, you know, I knew from reading this interview you did with Mealy that, you know, your mother's family were very musical and I was just curious to see if your father's family was the same way. They were too. Yeah, did you, like, did you have cousins on your father's side of the place? Yeah, one, well the

only one that took interest in it, his name, he was my first cousin's son, Gus, he called it. His name was Gus, but that's the rights. The rights? The rights, yeah. How do you spell that? W-R-I-G-H-T. With a W in front of him. Yeah. Well, he, he's in California now, he's digging up a drum, he was a drum player. That's the only one I remember that played on my father's side. Would you like me to tell you something about jazz? Or you want to ask some more questions? Ask some more questions.
Well, I have lots of questions to ask. Well, okay. But I want to know what you want to tell me about jazz. I've read your life story that you wrote for too late.

Well, that's not what I wanted to actually tell you about. Not myself. Oh, well tell me what you want to tell me about. I want to, you know, the important thing is what you have to say. Well, I'm going to tell you one of the curious things that I, uh, I found when I came back to New Orleans that so many of the old musicians actually forgot the difference between traditional jazz and New Orleans jazz. Oh, you mean they have forgotten it? They have forgotten. And, uh, they all confused and they call it all Dixieland jazz. Yeah. Which it is not. It is not. Is it all right to talk about that? Oh, it's fine. I'd love to talk about that. Sounds like a good subject. Well, I'll tell you the difference. You being, you're not being a musician, probably you wouldn't understand, but you will get an idea. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. traditional jazz or most music is the beat. See the traditional jazz music, the beat is like a parade, you see a parade beat. It's two beats to the bar. Now I'm going to give you an idea. That's traditional jazz. Dixieland jazz is four beats to the bar. The bass violin plays like a . This is a lot of jazz, the bass play. He's playing different. You see it's a different beat. The banjo and the piano, you play jazz, he's getting straight compliments with all fingers hitting. Now in Dixieland, a lot of Dixieland bands use summer, but sometimes the piano is running all over the piano while the band is playing. Oh yeah. Yeah I've heard of this. And the traditional jazz is giving the band a foundation. Now the band starts off like that. And they play like that until you get to the last chorus. When you get to the last chorus, the leader of the band, he may be a clarinet player, a trombone player, or a trumpet player, whoever he is, he hits his foot down, that let the men know he's going out, fixing to go out. Then the music changes, traditional jazz. Then we jump song the four beat, like I tell you, like the Dixieland, and the big song is going to be a little bit. And the drum, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. And he hits the cymbal, one beat, after beat they call out. Like the, dum, dum, dum, dum, dum, dum, dum, dum, dum, dum. You see? Yeah, I know that. But you don't make that beat, that's Dixieland beat. But it's one beat. Something like the people do in the church, a Baptist choice. Like to be saved. John the bell, done got over. John the bell. You understand? Yeah. Now when they do that, I don't know if you can pick it up. People used to hit this beat. Oh yeah. John the bell, done got over. Now that's where the Dixieland pick it up from there. Oh, I see. Yeah. But the traditional jazz put that, the the Dixieland, the hand, you see the hand. But it's not on the beat, you know, like people say, John the bell, done got over. Not like that, you see. As the pure races do that, most of the pure races. But the mixed race, we New Orleans people, they have the beat. You see? Don, the bell, done got over. John the bell. John got over. John the bell. John got over. John got over. John got over. John got over. John got over. John got over. John got over. At last. You see that after beat. Now the next thing about music, in traditional jazz, that tempo that I gave you, that's mostly what they use. They use a moderate tempo. And then they'll play slow blues tempo. A slow tempo for a song and then the slow blues and the boogie woogie. And the boogie woogie, there's no one who knows when that, that's just about as old as jazz. Oh really? I didn't know that. That's right. See we was talking about the Boogie Woogie Dixter Land and the parade beat jazz, but the boogie woogie is eight-beat. Mm-hm. Dumbled for . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . . So the Dixieland is fast music all the time. When we was young and we played mostly among the white race, they said, play it hot, play it hot.
What do they mean by play it hot?
They meant play it fast. Play some hot music. Play some hot music.
That's like four beats to a bar?

Yeah. It's fast. Dixieland. They used to like to jump fast, you know, but we wouldn't do that too regularly, now and then. And after we'd play a fast, we would play a waltz. People hardly ever asked for waltz. Back in those times they considered that was a very bad business. There wasn't much of a band if you didn't play a waltz.
When was this?
This was in the 20s?
When was this? That's before the 20s.
Before? Yeah, the 20s, that's when the Dixieland came in.
You're talking about like before the war, before World War?

Before the war. Before World War I. You see. When World War I come in then the bands, after that the bands start Dixieland music. Dixieland is traditional jazz, the last chorus of traditional jazz, you understand? Where we run into four beats and hit all the drum and the bass hitting boom, boom, boom, boom, boom, boom. Everything is, that's the, Dixieland is the last part of traditional jazz.
Oh I see.

Because the Dixieland music don't use traditional jazz at all. They start the band off right on four and on the cymbal you see, cha cha cha cha cha cha you don't have to be that sound about before. That's the Dixieland. They start that. But traditional jazz you weren't allowed to play, a new drum player wasn't allowed to jump on the cymbal when you start off. He had to play that snare drum. See they used to work plenty on the snare drum. It was very beautiful. And it's traditional jazz music, that's music that shakes you up more than any music. Yeah. Well you get quite a beat shaken out of Dixieland but that's the last part of it. When you play in Dixieland there's nothing to go to. But when you play traditional jazz, when you get to the last, then you jump to that four beat and it changes like another band coming. Can you get me? Yeah, I think I understand. And it would give you great inspiration. You get to the music and people get to shout. Yeah. It's quite different from bop and rock and roll because when you play bop music people sit down and listen, but when you're playing traditional jazz you can't sit so easy. Your feet's going or something. Yeah that's true.
Yeah.
It's something, if you have a little baby in there, the little baby will start dancing. I know.
You're right there.

And traditional jazz, most of the musicians don't be jumping around with the instruments, showing off and all that. They be straight trying to make you feel good. Traditional jazz is to make you get the feeling. Where the Dixland band come in, they want to make the people see how good they are.
Oh I see. So they show off.

Yeah. Like bop, they show off. They do the instruments, throw the instruments back ahead and do all kinds of things. You know, a real show that the people are not interested in the music, look how great I am, look what I can do with my instrument. See a traditional band is not that traditional jazz. It is to play to make you get the fire and inspiration. You don't be jumping around but be playing so hot that you can't keep still. You grab some, you call this dance, you know? And that's the difference. Anything else you want to ask me?
About traditional jazz I'd like to ask you, who did you play traditional jazz with in New Orleans? With what bands? Who was playing it before you went away?

Well, I started playing in a band actually in 1919. I was 17 years old and I was going on 18. I wouldn't be 18 in November of that year, in 1919, but I started playing a little before I got to my birthday so it actually made me start playing at 17. Oh that's pretty young.
Now we formed a band ourselves.

And I don't want to make it too long but I'll tell you some of the members of the band. On drumming we had Si Frasier, Josiah Frasier on drumming. On bass we had Eddie Barrera. On piano we had Mercedes Fields. On the trumpet we had Bush Hall. Well Bush Hall died and he was replaced with Red Alam. He had Red Alam. He had Darius Ballera. He had Darius Ballera. He had Darius Ballera. He had Darius Ballera. He had Darius Ballera. He had Darius Ballera. He had Darius Ballera. Darius Ballera. Darius Ballera. Darius Ballera.
Darius Ballera. Darius Ballera.

Darius Ballera. Darius Ballera. Darius Ballera. Darius Ballera. Darius Ballera. Darius Ballera. Darius Ballera. Darius Ballera. Darius Ballera. Darius Ballera. Darius Ballera. Darius Ballera. Darius Ballera. Darius Ballera. Darius Ballera. Yeah they take me to the end.
It really caught up.
And Johnny Handley heard me play saxophone and he was so enthused over my saxophone playing that he put his clarinet down and he then got him a saxophone.
I never knew that. I didn't know he picked that up there.

He was a wonderful clarinet player, Johnny Handley. He was a wonderful clarinet player. Everybody likes to hear him play clarinet plays. But he put the clarinet down and after he heard me with that sax he didn't have nothing with that clarinet anymore. And the poor fellow he died but he never could get back to his clarinet again.
Yeah, that happens to a lot of you. I'm surprised that didn't happen to you. You know, like Harold Dajon, Andrew Morgan, John Handley, and I'm surprised.

Well Morgan got him attacked. He came to me, Andrew, and take my lessons on the sax. Really? Yeah, Andrew Morgan. Because he was fooling with the clarinet too. But everybody was enthused over it. Everything was Paul Barnes, Paul Barnes. They quit calling me Pullo. Oh they did?
Yeah, I was Pullo.
I wonder why they quit there. Well when I started playing music they called me Paul in school. When I went to school they wouldn't use my nickname of Pullo Barnes. Oh I see.
Yeah, in school.
And just lately I started using Pullo Barnes Professional.
I'm just watching it to make sure the volume is okay. Oh yeah.

That's okay. So at the finish time you brought the band. So we had George Washington on trombone, a very good trombone player. We had a wonderful band, but we lost George and then we had Earl Humphrey, the one that's
playing with us now.

We had Earl. So Earl he left and he went away. And so we got a fellow called Thomas. Sorry I can't think of Thomas. He died three years ago. We got Thomas. And the band was playing real good, really good. So Kid Rene, he had the hottest jazz band around town.
Yeah?
Yeah, they had Sam Morgan, Chris Kelly, and Buddy P.T. But none of them could surpass Kid Rene. That's fabulous.
This was in 1919, around then.
Yeah, that's right. The oldest one that could outblow Rene or anybody else was Louis Armstrong.
Really? He was that good?

Oh yeah. Because see the best, the stiffest trumpet player we had around here was Freddie Capit. And then after him came King Oliver and South Stand and all the people. Freddie Capit was away. Freddie Capit left and went away. And Louis Armstrong came up and took charge. Because Louis used to hang around with Buddy P.T. And Buddy P.T. showed him a lot of stuff and he picked up Buddy P.T.'s style. And then he added the high notes to it because Buddy didn't play all those high notes. He made beautiful changes in all his stuff. He was one of the toughest things we had in New Orleans. But Rene didn't play that style. Rene played that other style of jazz. He had high notes too. And then Kid Rene. What do you mean that other style of jazz? You said he played that other style of jazz. What do you mean by that? You said Kid Rene?
Well they've got two styles. One fellow would play a style where he was making a lot of notes. My kid punched you. Oh yeah. Dadda dadda dadda. Yeah. All that.

You'd run all that too. And Buddy would run beautiful notes like that too. But Rene didn't use that. Rene punched out the melody and swang the melody. And swang the whole house too. Yeah? That's great. So when Rene heard me play, he was so enthused over my saxophone playing, he got me in the band. And that made it, he's there real great. Because there was a saxophone playing, and he was playing with me. And then afterwards they finally got saxophone. So finally a musician was an insurance collector and he told me, he said, you're too good to waste your time, why don't you join the Tuxedo band?
Yeah.

That was Celestad. Celestad and Pierron and they were big society bands, you see. And they'd make more money. So I joined Celestad's band, Tuxedo band. They'd heard Rene very much because he liked it so much. He hated it. But there was nothing you could do but I was making more money and everything else. So I worked with the Tuxedo band. And the Tuxedo band, that's what, that's called an original Tuxedo band. And that was long before my time, payback time, and Johnny Sincere, Kirok, we went out with nothing but a baby. The Tuxedo band was formed. So when I got in the band, around the last part of the Tuxedo band, and they came up with a little confusion between Ridgely, the manager of the band, and Papa Celestad. So Papa Celestad quit the band.
Oh I see, they had fallen out. I want to ask you, Paul, why did Ridgely and Celestad fall out? They just didn't agree about running the band?
Well that's the point I want to come to. In fact what went between those two people, none of us actually never do it, but it was something concerning a few dollars.
Oh it was money.

But anyway, we thought probably Celestad wasn't getting a right deal, but maybe Ridgely may be in the right, we actually don't know. But before Ridgely died they told me it was just concerning a little money. And it was a terrible mistake that they made because the band was too great. So I took Simon Marrera, John Marrera, and myself and Abbie Foster, Chinese we called him, drum player. We went over to Celestad's house and talked Celestad into making up his own band. And called it Celestad's original Tuxedo band. So Celestad said, well if you all want to be back with me I'll do it. So we formed Celestad's original Tuxedo band. But we couldn't get Emma Barrett, the one that people call the bell girl, we couldn't get her to leave.
Oh she stayed with them.

She stayed with Ridgely. So we had to get a piano player and in those times lady piano players were very popular with bands in those days. So we went across the lake and we met, I got a girl over there, Jeanette Sullivan, her name is. She got married to Norvin Kimball.
Oh yeah.

Jeanette Sullivan. So we got her to play in the band. And the band made a great success. The band then, I composed a number and we called it My Josephie. And the number made such a hit with the people that it actually swarmed Ridgely's Tuxedo. Really? By the way Ridgely called his band Ridgely's Tuxedo and Celestad called his band Papa Celestad's Tuxedo. But that Ridgely's Tuxedo band died out of the picture. And all that was left was Papa Celestad's Tuxedo band. So I stayed with Papa Celestad band. All that happened in 1925. And in 1927 that recording that I heard about, that I spoke to you about, My Josephine, when it got to Chicago, King Alba heard about the band. And the first thing he wondered who was that saxophone player doing all that play? Oh yeah. He wrote to a trumpet player called Manuel Perez. Manuel Perez and King Alba would be taking more musicians out of New Orleans than any other people. Because Manuel Perez would notice who was great. And the great ones he tells King Alba about.
Oh I see.
And King Alba was simply. So then.
Yeah, you stayed with Celestan, that became the best band.

Yeah, well anyway I played with Celestan's band after that until 1927, and King Oliver had heard that record of my Josephine, and was so enthused over the work that I did that at the manual parades, told him about it, and I left Papa Celestan's band, that was in 1927, and I got there and joined King Oliver's band in St. Louis, Missouri, Red Island and I left together. And them fellas liked me because I showed them all, I showed Red Island a lot on his trumpet, and it's like I showed Celestan too, and they liked me very much for that. So anyway, we left Missouri, played there in St. Louis, Missouri, and we went to New York, played the Savoy Ballroom with King Oliver's band. You want to hear some of the line up of those bands?
Yeah, the Savoy?

Well I'll give you a few of them. You see on piano we had Louis Russell on piano, and banjo, Willie Foster, that's Pop Foster's brother, on banjo. On drums we had Paul Barbaran on drums. And on bass we had a bass player called Buford. Now on trumpet we had King Oliver, Red Island, so far back I can't think of the boy's name. Yeah. That's what I remember. That's what I remember. That's what I remember. That's what I remember. That's what I remember. That's what I remember. That's what I remember. That's what I remember. That's what I remember. That's what I remember. That's what I remember. That's what I remember. That's what I remember. That's what I remember. That's what I remember. That's what I remember. That's what I remember. That's what I remember. Boy, he just died too, not so long ago.
Great kind of guy. Darnell Harris?

No. No, Darnell Harris, in fact Darnell Harris taken his place. Oh really? In Chicago. And you knew him too. Yeah, he went away to Paris, France with Wilbur. Oh, I love that. Wilbur to Paris. Simeon. Oh, Omar. Omar Simeon. Yeah, that was our read section. Well we had a good band and so I won't get off that, but the band broke up because we were supposed to go in the cotton club and King Oliver wanted too much money, so instead the band got Duke Ellington. And that's why King Oliver made his mistake, because his band didn't get working and he broke up. So after his band broke up I stayed around New York and I worked. Really? Yeah, I didn't come home. Ray Allen came back home. He came back later. But I stayed in New York, I stayed there about five years after that. But I played with practically all the great musicians around there. And I played with Alma Snowden, that's the one that had Duke Ellington play in his band, Alma Snowden. I played in that band. Then I played with Chick Webb. I wasn't a regular member of Chick Webb's band but I would do gigs with Chick Webb's band. And Louis Russell, what did I tell you, that piano player died, he recommended me to Jell-A-Roll-Martin. Oh Louis Russell did.
I see. That's how you got up with Jell-A. Yeah, that's how I got up with Jell-A-Roll-Martin. Because King Oliver's band broke up.

See, Bonnie Biggore went with Duke Oliver and Omar Simeone, he went with Earl Hines and I, Paul Barnes, went with Jell-A-Roll-Martin. But times were tough. I bet it was. When I got to New York it was just a little before Littborg flew across the ocean. Oh yeah? Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh. Oh.
Oh.

Oh dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear dear No, no, no, no, no, I didn't play in the band.
You were playing in night clubs?

Yes, I played in all of them, different night clubs, different bands. And finally in 1931 I joined King Oliver's band again and we made a tour, it was unsuccessful. I came back to New Orleans and stayed and then finally up to 34 I went off with King Oliver again from 35 now. Things was bad. Real bad?
Well that was a depression.

Yeah we wasn't making any money during the depression. So that's the end of King Oliver because he passed away in 35. He never did recover. Oh no, he was very, very hurt. I know all the trumpet players I played with, they all were just like me. They're like my first time I played. You can ask me what you want because I don't have any money.

Okay, well I wanted to ask you, I was curious about what was it like to travel around with a band then? Like nowadays the bands all travel around and they talk about, you know, it's pretty hard work on the road. I wonder what it was like in 1934 to travel around and trust.

It was pretty hard with us sometimes, with King Oliver's band, because we had plenty of trouble, bus break down and we weren't making any money. But it was a pleasure traveling with Yellow Room Martin. See because Yellow Room Martin had a big bus, a great big bus in there. Every member in the band had two seats we used to sit down and play checkers and play cards. Like rich people with Yellow Room Martin. But it was pretty tough with King Oliver. I bet.
Playing with the bands.
But still no, we didn't make any money with either of them. They just wanted money to be made.
I guess not, well I read your diary of where you went with King Oliver in 1934, little bitty towns and sometimes you wouldn't get paid. That's right. That must have been real hard.
It was really hard.
And I wanted to ask you, were there a lot of difference between your white audiences and your Negro ones?
Yeah. You all? We played, most of our work was with the white audiences.
Most of us?
Yeah. But they didn't have any money either. Yeah. So we played with the colored audiences and come out with a dollar and something, sometime a piece. The money wasn't there, that's all.
Yeah. Well did you have good crowds for your concerts?
Pretty fair, not too much. Not too much crowds. People didn't have the money to come out.
I guess they didn't for 1934. It was pretty bad. Well what did you all do when you were traveling around? What did you do when you weren't working? Did you just fool around?

That's all we do, just sit around waiting for a date. Stay somewhere a couple of days and we just go in and visit different friends, people that we'd meet, you know. They'd like to have us come and sit down and make nice drinks for us and all. We were treated right, but there just wasn't no money in it, you see. And we just couldn't go on like that. Those boys had families to take care of, you know. Yeah, I understand.
They just couldn't make it. But people treated you good, like you didn't run into a lot of race prejudice, there wasn't a lot of bad treatment in Muslim towns?

Well no, we didn't run into a lot of that. Probably the other people did, but everywhere we went they had great respect for us as musicians, you see. And the colored and white dance would never be together, you know, colored and white together. Very little of it, in fact, very little of it you saw up north.
Oh really? Was that the same up north?

Up north, because most of the mixing with the whites and colored would be in Harlem. The white people would come up and mix with the colored people. But there wasn't many of the colored people who would go down there and mix with them. Very few colored people would go, or mix with them.
So like when you were traveling with Jelly Roll you'd play one night for white people and then the next?

Another time, yeah, for colored people. But the white people always mix more, they'd mix more with the colored people, then the colored people would mix with them. For some reason it looked like it always was like that, I don't know. I wonder why? I just don't understand how.
Like you say in Harlem, you know, the white people would come into Harlem.
Yeah, a lot of white people would come up to Harlem, you know, but there wasn't too many colored people going out there.
But they would come up to Harlem to listen to music and go drinking and things?
Drinking, yeah, dance together, colored and white and everything. Probably, maybe the colored people wasn't making enough money to go downtown.
Maybe so.
In the white places, huh? Maybe so. I don't know what it was, but they didn't bother with it. I don't know how.

That's good. Yeah, I was just curious. Another thing I wanted to ask you, did you play on boats up and down like the Ohio River and the Kentucky River and rivers like that when you played with King Oliver?
No.
You didn't ever play on boats?

No, with none of them. Yeah, with him. Yeah, no, I never did play on boats. The only time I played on the boat was right here in New Orleans with Sidney Densene. Oh yeah. And we used to play on the Island Queen at the same boat that the government wanted to get rid of right now. Really? Yeah, I used to play on the Island Queen with Sidney Densene. Man, I played there a while. But it's a strange thing. I used to play plenty of schools. You called it the dance schools. You see, taxi dance, you used to call it. You have a ticket, you don't have time to make a dance. I played many of them school, but I have never, one time, see a colored person come in one of those dances. A taxi dance hall?
Yeah.
I have never seen one of those places for colored people. Really? That colored people have themselves.
Isn't that strange?

You go in there, you understand? Yeah. And every time you buy a certain amount of tickets, and every time you make a dance, play sharp, the band play sharp. Take a ticket, the girl take a ticket off. She'd give her the whole roll of taking that until the tickets are all gone. Then you go by and move and every time you play a dance, he takes a dance, keep on dancing. But never, never did I ever see a colored person or a colored girl even working up there. Isn't that strange?
Yeah.
I don't say they would hire them, but it actually looked like segregation, because I've never seen a colored girl work in those places. That's strange.
I've heard of the taxi dance schools, but I didn't know that they were awful. Well they've had them here too. Yeah.
But of course down here they were just the white, you understand? But you're talking about in the north you never saw them for colored people.
No, no. Well that's a peculiar thing.
Never seen a colored person even go in there and dance like that.
That's a very peculiar thing. A man or a woman.
Never heard of a colored girl ever going there and want a job to do that or anything like that.

That is strange. That's strange. Well did the musicians in the north live different? Like down here the musicians drink a lot and up there did they drink a lot or did they smoke a lot of tea and stuff like that? Or did they live different from when they lived down here?

No, same thing. They drink a lot and everything. Everything among the musicians is up there the same as down here. The only thing but they didn't embarrass them, they never caught any other views and don't. Really? But there may have been a few of them you know. Yeah. But very seldom they didn't come into contact. They thought that was terrible. Really? You see.
Well I've heard of a lot of musicians that smoke tea or marijuana and I just wondered if it was common.
Well they wasn't doing it at that time.
In the 20s?
Yeah, in the 20s no they wasn't doing it. There were some that were doing it though, but very few.
It wasn't an accepted thing.
It wasn't popular, no.
Like everybody drinks you know. That's popular.
Well see like now it's got to be common. Even down here and all you know they got common for them to take up that drink and smoke, they used to call that the tea you know.
Yeah.
They called it marijuana, they called it tea. So that's different.
I was just curious, you know I was wondering like if Jelly Roll and his musicians smoked tea and stuff like that. No. I was just curious. They didn't know that.
No, I had never seen one of them. But we all would drink though. Yeah they drank liquor.
Yeah.
But never had one of them in the band to bother with their smoke.
Yeah. That's really interesting because now like you say it is so popular and so common. I was just curious, you know that's something that is changing.
I remember one time we run into that, I believe it was in Kansas, but I was with King Oliver's band.
Where was this?
I was with King Oliver's band and through Kansas I believe it was. Oh Kansas, yeah.
Wow. So that's where you from?
No, I'm from Kentucky. Oh that's right, Kentucky.
Kentucky.

So we went, the fellow was selling weeds and things. So we went over there and bought some weeds just to get a kick out of it. Well we didn't get much of a kick out of it. But what I did, I brought some of the seeds home in New Orleans.
Oh yeah.
And I gave it to my brother, I said listen, and she said yeah, I'm going to plant it and see if it would grow.
Yeah, this is, whose brother was this?
Mealy. Mealy. Yeah, he said yeah let's plant it and see if it would grow. I said yeah we try. We plant the marijuana weed and the things start growing so fast so he got scared and destroyed it all.
He got scared?
Yeah. Really? Because he didn't think it would grow, you know. Oh I see. Those things grow up sometimes.
Oh isn't that funny?
Yeah, it was. He didn't want it to spread you know. Yeah he was going to have a big crop before he knew it.
Before he knew it you see. Well he destroyed it all. Isn't that funny?
Yeah. And Mealy destroyed all that stuff.
Yeah it was pretty dangerous stuff, you know they send you to jail if they catch you
grow up. But if the law had caught us though they wouldn't think that we would do enough experiments you
know. Oh yeah they think you're doing it to sell. To sell. We'd been in a world of trouble.
Yeah they send you to Angola for that stuff. Yeah. That's funny. Well I guess it just wasn't as important then as it is now to smoke tea or dope or anything.

I mean I think it's really hard for now. Well I've had quite a bit of experience in music. I've played with so many of the great musicians. I've played with Johnny Sincere and Kid Ory. I forgot to tell you about the trombone player.
Kid Ory was our trombone player when we went to New York. Oh at the Savoy? At the Savoy Ballroom.
Yeah I forgot to mention him.
And the trumpet player that I couldn't remember his name, that was Grey. Yeah his name was Grey. Yeah his name was Gray.
Thomas Gray?
I believe it was something like that. Sorry, it just come to me. Gray. But I think you all already have that.
Already did? Yeah. I don't remember. That's fascinating. I was just curious because you have traveled with bands both in the south and in the north and out west.

Well through my life I can see I had an opportunity to play with almost all the great musicians. We were playing together in Louis Russell's band. We had Johnny Hodges, old saxophone with us you know. And I played four years at Disneyland. And we had Johnny Sincere, he's passed. We had the great Monet Moore singing, she's passed. And then we had Louis Armstrong playing with us. He's sick now, he hardly playing anymore. And Johnny Sincere, famous banjo, that was Louis Hot Five, you know. Oh yeah. Johnny Sincere, well he was playing banjo. And on the piano, they had Harvin Brooks, used to be Mamie Smith, you ever heard of Mamie Smith? Oh yes. But I was a hot piano player one time, Harvin Brooks. We had a real good, we had Mike Dilley on trumpet. And on drum we had Alton Red. We had a real good band out at Disneyland. I worked up there four years.
Well something I wanted to ask you, you know, you played so much saxophone with all the big bands, why did you take that clarinet again?
Well I'm going to tell you why I got interested. I used to play a little bit clarinet before I played sax, you know.
Yeah, you told me that.

So I put it down completely and like handed it, I put it down and I picked up on soprano sax. I used to play that with the, in the place of clarinet in General Rowe Martin's band. But I played clarinet with King Oliver's band, but I didn't play it like I played on here. I just played the big arrangement, where you put down the clarinet and play a part and you grab up the soprano sax, and then you change to L or like that. I didn't take a whole lot of, no special solos like I do now with the clarinet. But what put me back on the clarinet, I joined the Navy. And I started the clarinet and I became so, I started progressing so fast on the clarinet. And then I was too much for second class to be first class musicians.
Oh good, I'm clarinet.
And that's about as high as you could go, no matter who you was, you couldn't go anymore in first class. The prejudice was so strong here.
Oh really?
Yeah, they wouldn't let a colored musician go in first class. Oh I didn't know that.
This was in the Navy here. Right in the Navy here.

It's not like that now, they kind of broke away from that. So if you wanted to go higher, you'd have to leave here with this Navy and maybe go to Cuba or something like that. Oh I see. But first class is as high as you could get, and that's as far as I went in the Navy. But I learned to play a lot of classics, operatic music and all that. Oh you did? I didn't know that. See I played all that. While you were in the Navy?
In the Navy.
In the Navy. I became the most outstanding clarinet player they had.
Oh that's great.
And I was the first top man instructing, showing the fellas to help them out. So we played all William Tell and all that kind of stuff.
Oh really? Yeah that's real classical. No we played all that.

Very. Morning, morning, night, great stuff like that. But we had an orchestra we could call, a sixteen or seven piece band that we used to play for dances for the sailors you know. Every Saturday night we played dance, something like that to that. But most of our work was classical work.
Who did you play the classical music for?
The symphonic work, symphony you know?
Oh really? It was like a symphony. Yeah.
Like symphony.
Oh it wasn't dances, people. And we had parades too.

You see, they'd commission ships like that. And we'd parade. Oh I see. Actually me and me played in three kinds of bands. That's right. Parades where we'd walk and parade and then we'd play dances, and dance bands, we had another band for that, and then we had a band to play all that classic, operatic symphonic.
I did not know it was so complicated playing in the Navy. I certainly didn't know you played concert music.
Oh yeah.
Yeah. But did you continue to play concert music after you got out of the Navy?

No. Never played one time. There is no, well now I could put an application to play in the concert here if I wanted some of these bands here because the prejudice is, you know, kind of people getting away from that. This country is trying to get together. White colored, white, blacks, and everybody wanted to try to work together. They began to learn that we all, no one actually is any better than the other fellow. And they began to learn that. But in them times the black people always thought that they were better than the white people. And the white people thought they were better than the blacks, you see.
Yeah. Everybody had their ideas. Yeah.
Now they began to realize that actually no one is any better. Just your environment weaves your life in a way.
Mm-hmm. That's true.
You being in the company, you let you come up, your ways and everything changed about you. Either for good or for bad. I agree. Well that's just of an end now. Well let's see there.

A couple more things I wanted to ask you. Oh something that was curious to me. As a woman I wanted to ask you, and this is just something I think about every now and then, why don't women ever play jazz music? Except for piano. Why is that? Do you know?
You know that's one question I don't think anyone can know.
Uh-huh.
But do you know that a woman can actually do anything a man can do?
No, I didn't know that.

That's right, anything. A man may have more strength in his body than her, but the way the world is going now, you don't need strength. You need brains. Amen. And so a woman, first being asked me that question, you hear a lot about the woman's liberation. To me that sounds like a lot of foolishness. Because a woman is at liberty as much as a man. Men don't have to give her no liberty, liberation. When you've got your voting power you've got everything. The women, they've got more women than men in this country. They can vote the men after the UN's presidency, the war. They can't accept the war.
Yeah.

And they can take over and build their own factories and hire men and all. There's nothing stopping me. No law means that a woman can't have a factory or something. Well that's true. Yeah, they're calling it, they don't give them, the men don't give them jobs and the men don't have to. They can vote the factory and give the man a job. That's what I see. I think you're right.
But did you ever know of women who played music, you know jazz music, I don't mean to
play a song?
They have a few of them.

In California they had a woman that was a trumpet player when I left out Los Angeles. Well they've got a few of them that played good trumpet, they've got a few women bands. But somehow or another, what we don't understand is a woman just don't care to do those things. Carpenters, bricklayers, women can do all that but they'd rather stay home and fix up the house. Yeah, I agree with you. Yeah, they'd rather do that and take care of the children. The men, he resents that. And each goes to what they like.
It isn't that a man can't.
A man can take care of the children and put diapers on it and feed it.
A lot of them do.

Yeah, he can do everything that women do. And why is it they don't take up the instruments? Most of them will take up the piano. They don't want to be bothered with it. They've got a few of the girls now that take up the piano, but when they leave school, they're finished.

Yeah, I just wondered because like when I go to a classical symphony, there are a lot of women who play in a classical symphony. They play violin, they play bass violin, and they play the triangle and they'll play the flute and the oboe and things like that in a concert symphony but never in jazz bands.
They just don't care for it. Isn't that strange?
Yeah.
They play a piano or something like that you know. But somehow or another they just don't get interested in it. It ain't that we tell them that no you can't play it because you're a lady.
They just don't take it. Yeah, well jazz seems to really be a man jazz.
It's like now you take a harp. You didn't notice most of the women playing those harps?
Yeah.
But you've got to see a man playing a harp, huh?
I don't know if I heard that.

Yeah, very simple. But there ain't no reason why he shouldn't play it. But he don't follow the harp. But a lady will play the harp. I know it's a symphony band. I always have them ladies, the men who have to do it.
Yeah, and even in modern jazz and rock and roll and things like that women don't play that. No.
You know, even nowadays.
And they just don't want to play it. They don't want to have anything to do it. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. If it would be to women, you know we wouldn't have any war.
Really?
We wouldn't have any war.
Why not? Why do you think that?
Because women are not interested in war.
No, they're not interested in war.
That's true.
Yeah, I'm not interested in war.
No, they've got a few of them that get interested in that, very few like Israel.
They've got Miss Mayer, is that her name?
Yeah, something like that. But she's like the president.
Yeah.
But very seldom. We have had queens, you know, back in history that run the things.
It's about done.

It's about done. It's about done. So I just don't see, it looks like the nature of a woman is just different from a man. But you take a child, you put plenty of toys, just put toys all around there. Those little boys will go grab and they'll get interested in that hammer, that saw, and that nutrain. And those girls will get interested in the dolls. Naturally, you don't have to give it to them, you know. They'll just take to that. They'll play with the airplane and things like the boys. They don't take that interest.
Yeah, you know, it does seem just to be nature.

I'm going to tell you something about a woman and a man that you didn't know. A woman likes beauty. And that's why this world is so beautiful today, because of the women, not the men. The men like comforts. As long as something is comfortable, he's right. But a woman will suffer pain is for beauty. It's like they used to put on tight upon corsets and all that. Oh yeah. Just because they're that beautiful. Having corsets and manors. When I was a kid, a woman wouldn't go out and put a garbage can out without a corset. And they wouldn't go to dance. She had to go to dance. The man had to put his hand on her like that. Oh, they thought that was awful. She didn't have a corset on. She better have a corset on.
Yeah.

So that's just the ways of a woman. And if you go to a camp where there's a man, the camp is just playing. But if the women had that camp, that camp would be beautifully painted up and curtains up and that's facts. Yeah. Have curtains up. I guess they'd put ribbons on the cows and things. I think so. Yeah, they'd put ribbons and bows on the cows. I think so. And pink the bells different colors that the cows wear on. Everything.
That's why the world is so beautiful.
It's for the women. See that?
Oh, that's beauty to be.
Man, you speak box. Just be comfortable. Yeah. When they ask you anymore. Mm-hm. Mm-hm. I want to agree with you.
Well, this one, I think we're about to move.
Thank you. Thank you.
